content: Furazolidone is a nitrofuran-class antibacterial agent. It is commercially available under the brand name Furoxone, marketed by Roberts Laboratories, and as Dependal-M, marketed by GlaxoSmithKline. Other brand names include Diafuron and Medaron. Furazolidone has applications in both human and veterinary medicine. It exhibits a broad spectrum of antimicrobial activity. It is effective against Gram-positive bacteria such as Clostridium perfringens, Corynebacterium pyogenes, Streptococci, and Staphylococci. It is also active against Gram-negative bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Salmonella dublin, and Salmonella typhimurium. Additionally, it has activity against protozoa, such as Giardia lamblia, Eimeria species, and Histomonas meleagridis. In humans, furazolidone has been used to treat diarrhea and enteritis caused by bacterial or protozoal infections. It has been employed in the management of traveler's diarrhea, cholera, and bacteremic salmonellosis. Its potential use in treating Helicobacter pylori infections has also been proposed. Furazolidone is used for giardiasis caused by Giardia lamblia, although it is not considered a first-line treatment. As with all medications, the most recent local guidelines and recommendations should be followed when prescribing or using furazolidone. The typical adult dosage is 100 mg four times daily, usually for 2–5 days, but treatment may extend up to 7 days in some cases or 10 days for giardiasis. For pediatric patients, the dosage is 25 mg/kg four times daily, with similar treatment durations. In veterinary medicine, furazolidone has been used with some success to treat infections caused by Myxobolus cerebralis in salmonids. It has also been utilized in aquaculture. However, as a nitrofuran antibiotic, its use in food-producing animals is prohibited by the FDA under the Animal Medicinal Drug Use Clarification Act of 1994. In laboratory settings, furazolidone is used to differentiate between micrococci and staphylococci. The mechanism of action of furazolidone is believed to involve the crosslinking of DNA, which disrupts bacterial and protozoal replication. Furazolidone is no longer available in the United States. While it is an effective antibiotic, particularly against infections resistant to other treatments, it is associated with numerous side effects. These include systemic toxicity at minimum inhibitory concentrations, manifesting as tremors, convulsions, peripheral neuritis, gastrointestinal disturbances, and suppression of spermatogenesis. Like other nitrofurans, furazolidone has been recognized by the FDA as a mutagen and carcinogen. Consequently, its use has been banned in the United States since 1991.
